Pregnancy

Vaccines During Pregnancy: Which Shots and When

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most pregnant people are advised to get up to four vaccines during pregnancy: Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, a flu shot in any trimester during flu season, COVID-19 vaccination at any point, and the RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season. Tdap and the RSV shot exist mainly for your baby, because the antibodies you build cross the placenta and protect your newborn before their own vaccines begin. The flu and COVID-19 shots protect you first, since pregnancy makes both illnesses more likely to turn severe, and they pass some protection to your baby as well. Live vaccines such as MMR and chickenpox are the ones that wait until after delivery. Here is how each shot works and how to map the timing onto your own calendar.

Why vaccines in pregnancy protect your baby

Your baby is born with almost no immune protection of their own, and most of their vaccines cannot start right away. Vaccines during pregnancy work around that gap. After each shot, your body builds antibodies, and those antibodies cross the placenta in the following weeks. Your baby arrives with borrowed protection that covers the earliest, most vulnerable months, exactly when infections like whooping cough and RSV are most dangerous to them. The timing of each shot is chosen so that antibody transfer peaks before birth. Your baby's own vaccine schedule begins later and is a separate topic; this guide covers only the shots you receive while pregnant.

The vaccines recommended in pregnancy are inactivated or protein-based. None of them contain live virus, and none of them can cause the illness they protect against. Flu and Tdap shots have been given to pregnant people for many years, and safety monitoring continues for every vaccine in the lineup. The most common side effects are a sore arm, tiredness, and sometimes a low fever for a day or two. Your own clinician knows your history, your allergies, and your due date, so treat every timing window here as the starting point for that conversation.

Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, in every pregnancy

Tdap protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis, better known as whooping cough. Whooping cough can be severe in newborns, who may struggle to breathe during coughing spells and often need hospital care if they catch it in the first weeks of life. ACOG and the CDC recommend one Tdap dose in every pregnancy, given between 27 and 36 weeks. Many clinicians aim for the earlier part of that window, because antibodies take about two weeks to build and transfer, and an earlier dose gives more time before birth. If your baby is likely to arrive early, ask whether to schedule the shot sooner within the window.

You need the shot again in each pregnancy, even if your last dose was recent, because antibody levels fall over time and each baby needs a fresh supply. If the window passes without a dose and you have never had Tdap before, you can still receive it right after delivery. That protects you from catching and passing on whooping cough, although your baby gets less direct benefit than from a dose during pregnancy. It also helps to ask partners, grandparents, and other close caregivers to check that their own pertussis vaccination is current. The people who will hold your newborn the most are also the most likely sources of infection.

The flu shot and the COVID vaccine while pregnant

The inactivated flu shot is recommended in any trimester and is considered safe throughout pregnancy. Pregnancy changes your heart, lungs, and immune system in ways that make flu more likely to become severe, so the shot protects you first. It also passes antibodies to your baby, which matters because infants under six months are too young for their own flu vaccine. If you are pregnant during flu season, usually fall and winter, get the shot when it becomes available rather than waiting for a particular week. One version to skip: the nasal spray flu vaccine is a live vaccine and is not used in pregnancy.

COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy is recommended by ACOG and other major maternal health groups, and it can be given at any point. Pregnancy raises the risk of severe COVID-19 illness, and vaccination lowers that risk for you while passing some protection to your baby for the early months. Guidance on updated doses changes from season to season, so ask your clinician which formulation applies to you and when to get it. It is fine to receive the COVID-19 vaccine at the same visit as other pregnancy shots. If you had COVID-19 recently, mention that too, since your clinician may suggest a short wait before the next dose.

The RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks

RSV is a common respiratory virus that usually causes a cold in adults but can cause serious breathing problems in young babies, and it is a leading reason infants are admitted to hospital. The maternal RSV vaccine is given once, between 32 and 36 weeks, and only during RSV season, which the CDC defines as roughly September through January in most of the continental United States. Local timing varies, so your clinic will follow the season in your region. The shot prompts your body to make antibodies that cross the placenta and protect your baby through their first RSV season, when the risk is highest.

There is an alternative pathway. Instead of the vaccine during pregnancy, your baby can receive an antibody injection, often called nirsevimab, shortly after birth or before their first RSV season. In most cases a baby needs one form of protection or the other, not both. Which one fits better depends on your due date, the local season, and availability, so this is a genuine conversation to have with your clinician rather than a fixed rule. One timing detail worth knowing: the maternal vaccine needs about two weeks before birth to transfer enough antibody, so if your baby arrives sooner than that, the infant antibody shot usually steps in.

Which vaccines are not safe during pregnancy

Live vaccines wait until after delivery. That includes MMR, which covers measles, mumps, and rubella, the varicella vaccine for chickenpox, and the nasal spray flu vaccine. These use weakened live viruses, and although harm from accidental doses appears to be very rare, waiting is the standard precaution. If early pregnancy bloodwork shows you are not immune to rubella or chickenpox, the usual plan is to vaccinate right after delivery, and these shots are considered compatible with breastfeeding. Ideally that catch-up is handled before pregnancy at a preconception visit. If you received a live vaccine before you knew you were pregnant, tell your clinician rather than assuming the worst.

A little preparation makes the vaccine conversation quick. Bring your vaccination record if you have one, or ask a previous clinic or pharmacy to send it. Mention any travel plans, since travel vaccines need an individual decision that weighs the destination against your stage of pregnancy. Flag allergies and any past reaction to a vaccine. It helps to note shot dates, side effects, and questions in the BeMama app or on paper so nothing gets lost between visits. Afterward, a sore arm and a tired day are normal. Call your clinician for a fever that stays high or redness that keeps spreading, and call emergency services for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or hives spreading over the body, which usually appear within minutes to hours of the shot.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Vaccines and medicines in pregnancy are chosen by weighing the risks of infection or untreated illness against the known information about a product. Recommended vaccines vary by pregnancy stage, season, location, and health history.

Do not start, stop, or change a prescription, over-the-counter medicine, herbal product, or supplement solely because of an online list. Product names and formulations can differ, and individualized review matters.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep a current medicine and vaccination list and save questions for a pharmacist or prenatal professional. The app does not verify interactions or safety.

When to seek help

Seek immediate care for a severe allergic reaction, trouble breathing, facial swelling, collapse, or another emergency. Contact the prescriber before stopping essential medicine.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks.
  • The inactivated flu shot is safe in any trimester and is worth getting early in flu season.
  • ACOG recommends COVID-19 vaccination, which can be given at any point in pregnancy.
  • The RSV vaccine is given at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season, or your baby can get an antibody shot after birth instead.
  • Live vaccines such as MMR and chickenpox wait until after delivery.

Frequently asked questions

What vaccines do you need when pregnant?

Most pregnant people need up to four: Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks, a flu shot in any trimester during flu season, COVID-19 vaccination at any point, and the RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks in season. Your clinician may adjust the list for allergies, travel, or timing. Everything else, including live vaccines like MMR, usually waits until after delivery.

What week of pregnancy do you get the Tdap vaccine?

Tdap is given between 27 and 36 weeks, and earlier in that window is often preferred so antibodies have time to build and cross the placenta before birth. You need a dose in every pregnancy, even if your last one was recent. If the window passes and you have never had Tdap, you can still receive it right after delivery.

Is the flu shot safe during pregnancy?

Yes, the inactivated flu shot is recommended in any trimester and has a long record of use in pregnancy. It protects you from severe flu and passes antibodies to your baby for their first months. The nasal spray version is a live vaccine and is not used in pregnancy.

When is the RSV vaccine given during pregnancy?

The maternal RSV vaccine is given once, between 32 and 36 weeks, and only during RSV season, roughly September through January in most of the continental United States. If the timing does not line up, your baby can receive an RSV antibody injection after birth instead. Ask your clinician which pathway fits your due date and local season.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
